questions.title: Diagnosing a deadlock between two ETL jobs
questions.prompt: Two nightly stored procedures occasionally fail with a deadlock error when they run at overlapping times, each updating the same two tables. Explain what a deadlock is, how SQL Server resolves it automatically, and two concrete things you'd change to prevent it from recurring.
questions.modelAnswer: Blocking happens whenever one transaction needs a lock another transaction already holds, and simply waits -- this is normal and expected. A deadlock is the special case where Transaction A is waiting on a lock held by Transaction B, while B is simultaneously waiting on a lock held by A -- neither can ever proceed. SQL Server detects this automatically and picks one transaction as the 'deadlock victim,' rolling it back and raising an error, while the other transaction proceeds normally. To prevent recurrence: (1) access the two tables in the same order in both procedures -- a common deadlock cause is two transactions locking the same two tables in opposite order; and (2) keep transactions as short as possible, doing only what genuinely needs to be atomic inside BEGIN/COMMIT, so locks are held for the shortest possible window and the overlap that triggers the deadlock has a smaller chance of occurring.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by reassuring whoever's asking that blocking itself isn't a bug -- it's how isolation is enforced any time two transactions genuinely need the same data at the same moment. A deadlock is the specific, more serious case: A is waiting on a lock B holds, B is waiting on a lock A holds, and neither can ever win -- it's a true standoff. SQL Server doesn't just hang forever; it detects the cycle and picks a 'deadlock victim' to roll back automatically, which is why the application sees an error and needs to retry. For the actual fix, the first thing I'd check is whether both procedures touch the two tables in a different order -- that's the single most common cause, and standardizing the access order so both procedures always touch, say, Table A before Table B usually eliminates it outright. Second, I'd look at whether either transaction is doing more than it needs to inside BEGIN/COMMIT -- unrelated reads, validation logic -- and trim the transaction down to just the atomic part, since shorter transactions hold locks for less time and collide less often.
commonMistakes: Treating a deadlock the same as ordinary blocking -- blocking is normal, a deadlock is a genuine, unresolvable standoff
Assuming SQL Server will just hang forever instead of recognizing it auto-detects and resolves deadlocks
Fixing the symptom by adding a retry loop in the application without addressing the inconsistent table access order
Making a transaction longer by adding error handling or logging inside it, which increases lock duration
keyPoints: Blocking is normal; a deadlock is two transactions waiting on each other with no way out
SQL Server auto-detects deadlocks and rolls back a chosen 'victim' transaction
The victim's application should retry the transaction
Accessing tables in a consistent order across procedures prevents most deadlocks
Shortening transactions reduces how long locks are held and how often collisions occur

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes blocking from a deadlock
Correctly explains SQL Server's automatic deadlock resolution

questions.title: A query got slow after it used to be fast
questions.prompt: A report query that filters WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013 used to run instantly and now takes minutes as the table has grown. There is an index on OrderDate. Diagnose why the index isn't helping, and rewrite the WHERE clause so it is.
questions.modelAnswer: The predicate is non-SARGable: wrapping the OrderDate column in the YEAR() function forces SQL Server to compute YEAR(OrderDate) for every single row before it can compare against 2013, which means the index on the raw OrderDate column can't be used -- it stores actual dates, not year-extracted values. This was barely noticeable on a small table (a full scan of a few hundred rows is instant either way), but as the table grows into the millions of rows, the same non-SARGable predicate turns a sub-second query into one that takes minutes. The fix is to rewrite the condition so the column itself is left untouched, and transform the comparison value instead: WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2014-01-01'. This asks the identical logical question but lets SQL Server use the index on OrderDate to jump directly to the matching range.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a textbook SARGability problem, and the giveaway is right there in the WHERE clause -- there's a function wrapped around the column. Any time I see YEAR(SomeDateColumn), UPPER(SomeColumn), or similar, my first instinct is: the index on that raw column can't be used, because SQL Server would have to transform every row's value before it could compare it, and an index doesn't store transformed values. The reason it 'used to be fast' is simply table size -- a full scan is invisible on a small table and brutal on a large one, so this kind of bug often doesn't show up until data volume grows past some threshold. The fix is always the same shape: stop transforming the column, and transform the comparison value instead. Instead of asking 'what year is this date in,' I ask 'is this date within the 2013 calendar year range' -- same answer, but now the raw OrderDate column is untouched in the comparison, so the existing index can be used for a range scan instead of a full scan.
commonMistakes: Blaming the index itself ('the index must be corrupt/fragmented') instead of the predicate wrapping the column
Rewriting to BETWEEN '2013-01-01' AND '2013-12-31' and accidentally excluding rows with a time component on Dec 31
Not recognizing other common non-SARGable patterns like UPPER(column) = 'X' or a leading-wildcard LIKE '%text'
Assuming the problem only appears with YEAR() and missing that any function on the column causes the same issue
keyPoints: SARGable means the predicate can use an index directly; non-SARGable forces a full scan
Wrapping the column in a function (YEAR, UPPER, etc.) makes a predicate non-SARGable
Fix by transforming the comparison value instead of the column
The performance gap only becomes visible as table size grows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the predicate as non-SARGable and explains why
Correctly explains why this matters more as the table grows
Provides a correct, equivalent SARGable rewrite

questions.title: A measure is ignoring the report's slicer selections
questions.prompt: A measure called 'West Region Sales' was written as CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), Geography[Region] = "West"). When a user applies a slicer on Geography[State] set to multiple East Coast states, the measure still shows West region totals instead of narrowing further. Explain why, and how you'd fix it if the intent is for the measure to respect both the hardcoded region condition and the slicer together.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a column mismatch, not a CALCULATE overwrite problem in the way it first appears -- the measure filters Geography[Region], while the slicer filters Geography[State], a different column entirely, so there's nothing for CALCULATE to overwrite; the measure's filter on Region and the slicer's filter on State both remain active simultaneously, and the combination (West region AND East Coast states) likely returns an empty or near-empty result, which can look like the measure is 'ignoring' the slicer when it's actually honoring an impossible intersection. The real fix depends on intent: if Region and State should interact at all, the model likely needs the measure's logic reconsidered -- for instance, if the actual intent was ever for CALCULATE to override a same-column filter, KEEPFILTERS would make a new filter combine with (intersect) an existing one on the same column instead of overwriting it, but that only applies when both filters target the same column, which isn't the case here. The practical fix is recognizing the filters are on different columns and adjusting the DAX to filter on the column that's actually meant to interact with the slicer, or removing the hardcoded Region condition if State should be the only filter that matters.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check is whether the measure's filter and the slicer's filter are even on the same column, because that's the detail that changes the whole diagnosis. Here they're not -- the measure hardcodes Geography[Region] = "West", and the slicer is on Geography[State]. CALCULATE's overwrite-by-default behavior only kicks in when a new filter targets a column that's already filtered; since Region and State are different columns, both filters stay active at the same time, which means the measure is actually doing exactly what it's coded to do -- show West region sales, further restricted to whichever East Coast states happen to also be in the West region (probably none, hence a confusing near-empty or unexpected result). This is a case where I'd go back to the business requirement rather than reach for KEEPFILTERS, because KEEPFILTERS solves same-column conflicts, and this isn't one. If the real intent was for the slicer to be the only thing controlling region/state filtering, I'd remove the hardcoded Region condition from the measure entirely rather than trying to patch the filter interaction.
questions.example:
-- The problem: two different columns filtered simultaneously, not a same-column overwrite
West Region Sales = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), Geography[Region] = "West")
-- Slicer filters Geography[State] (East Coast states) -- a different column,
-- so both filters stay active together, likely producing an empty intersection.

-- If the true intent is for the slicer alone to control the result:
Region Sales = SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]) -- no hardcoded CALCULATE filter at all
commonMistakes: Assuming the measure 'isn't respecting' the slicer because of CALCULATE's overwrite behavior, when the real issue is two different columns both staying active
Reaching for KEEPFILTERS as a fix without checking whether the two filters even target the same column
Not recognizing that an unexpected near-empty result can be the system behaving correctly against a flawed assumption
Fixing the symptom by changing the slicer instead of questioning whether the hardcoded Region filter belongs in the measure at all
keyPoints: CALCULATE's overwrite-vs-combine behavior only applies to filters on the same column
A measure filtering one column and a slicer filtering a different column both stay active together
An unexpected result can mean the filters are correctly combining into an impossible intersection
The fix should match actual business intent, not just reflexively apply KEEPFILTERS or REMOVEFILTERS

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies that Region and State are different columns, both staying active
Correctly explains why this isn't a CALCULATE overwrite scenario
Proposes a fix grounded in actual business intent rather than a reflexive KEEPFILTERS/REMOVEFILTERS patch

questions.title: A report is hanging, but there's no deadlock error
questions.prompt: Users report that a dashboard query has been 'just spinning' for several minutes, but no deadlock error ever appears. Explain the difference between this situation and a deadlock, how you'd identify the actual head blocker, and what you'd check before deciding to kill the blocking session.
questions.modelAnswer: This is ordinary blocking, not a deadlock -- a deadlock is a genuine standoff that SQL Server detects and resolves automatically within seconds by killing a victim; it never just hangs indefinitely. Plain blocking, by contrast, can hang as long as whatever is holding the lock keeps holding it, because there's no cycle for SQL Server to detect -- one session is simply waiting its turn behind another, and nothing resolves that automatically. To find the actual head blocker, I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests, specifically looking at the blocking_session_id column -- the session with a non-zero blocking_session_id is being blocked, and the session that ID points to (which itself usually shows blocking_session_id = 0) is the head blocker actually holding the lock everyone's waiting on. Before killing that session, I'd check what it's actually doing -- its SQL text, and whether it's an open, uncommitted transaction (an application that opened a transaction and is sitting idle, or a long-running batch job that's legitimately mid-write). Killing a session mid-write rolls back whatever it was doing, which can be worse than the wait itself if it's a large, mostly-finished operation -- so I'd rather understand what it's doing and consider letting it finish or committing/rolling it back cleanly than reflexively kill it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd clarify, because it changes the whole response, is that this isn't a deadlock -- SQL Server resolves deadlocks on its own, usually within seconds, by picking a victim and rolling it back. If nothing has errored and the query is just sitting there, that's plain blocking: one session waiting on a lock another session is holding, with no cycle, so nothing forces a resolution automatically. My first query is always against sys.dm_exec_requests, looking at blocking_session_id -- that tells me directly who's blocked and, by following the chain, who the actual head blocker is, as opposed to the session that looks blocked but is itself only blocked by someone else further up. Once I've got the head blocker's session ID, I'd pull its actual SQL text and check whether it's sitting inside an open transaction that was never committed, versus genuinely mid-execution on a big write. That distinction decides what I do next -- if it's an application bug that opened a transaction and forgot to close it, killing the session is reasonable and I'd also flag that bug separately. If it's a legitimate long-running batch load that's 90% done, killing it rolls back all of that work and probably makes things worse, so I'd rather let it finish, or coordinate with whoever owns that job before touching it.
questions.example:
-- Find who's blocking whom
SELECT session_id, blocking_session_id, wait_type, wait_time, status
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests
WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0;

-- Follow the chain to the head blocker (blocking_session_id = 0, but others point to it)
-- Then inspect what the head blocker is actually running:
SELECT text
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests r
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) t
WHERE r.session_id = @HeadBlockerSessionId;
commonMistakes: Treating any hanging query as a deadlock, when a true deadlock is auto-resolved within seconds, not left hanging
Killing the first blocked session found instead of tracing blocking_session_id to the actual head blocker
Killing a session without checking whether it's mid-write on a legitimate long-running job
Not distinguishing an application bug (an abandoned open transaction) from a genuinely busy, legitimate session
keyPoints: A hanging query with no error is ordinary blocking, not a deadlock -- deadlocks auto-resolve quickly
sys.dm_exec_requests' blocking_session_id column traces the blocking chain to the actual head blocker
Check what the head blocker is actually doing before killing it -- an abandoned transaction vs. a legitimate long write
Killing a session mid-write rolls back its work, which can be worse than waiting for it to finish

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes ordinary blocking from a deadlock
Correctly identifies how to find the head blocker (sys.dm_exec_requests / blocking_session_id)

Provides correct, relevant diagnostic SQL

questions.title: A Covering Index Isn't Helping, and Nobody Knows Why
questions.prompt: A table has a nonclustered index covering exactly the columns a report query needs, but the query's execution plan still shows a full scan instead of using the index. The query is SELECT * FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail WHERE ProductID = 712. What's the most likely cause, and how would you fix the query?
questions.modelAnswer: SELECT * is almost certainly the cause. A covering index only helps when the query asks for columns the index actually includes; SELECT * asks for every column in the table, regardless of what's actually needed, which defeats the index's coverage the moment even one requested column isn't part of it. SQL Server then has to fall back to either a Key Lookup for each matching row or a full scan, depending on cost, instead of satisfying the query entirely from the narrower index. The fix is to name only the columns the report genuinely needs instead of SELECT *: SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty, UnitPrice FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail WHERE ProductID = 712. If those four columns are exactly what the covering index includes, the optimizer can now satisfy the entire query from the index alone, without ever touching the underlying table.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before touching the index, I'd actually look at the execution plan and the exact columns requested, because 'should use the index but doesn't' almost always traces back to the SELECT list, not the index definition. SELECT * is the first thing I'd check, because it's such a common habit and such a direct cause: if the index only covers four specific columns and the query asks for all fifteen columns on the table via *, the index simply can't satisfy that request on its own, and SQL Server has to go fetch the rest from the table itself — either via a Key Lookup per row or by abandoning the index entirely for a full scan, depending on how many rows are involved. The fix is almost always just naming the specific columns the report actually displays instead of *. I'd also double check that the index's included columns genuinely match what the report needs, because if even one required column is missing from the index, the same fallback happens no matter how narrowly I write the SELECT list.
commonMistakes: Assuming the index itself must be broken or missing, without checking what columns the query actually requests
Rebuilding or recreating the index before checking the SELECT list, missing the actual cause
Not verifying the index's included columns genuinely cover everything the trimmed SELECT list needs
Fixing this one query but not checking other queries against the same table for the identical SELECT * habit
keyPoints: SELECT * requests every column, defeating a covering index that only includes some of them
The fallback is a Key Lookup per row, or a full scan, instead of satisfying the query from the index alone
The fix is naming exactly the columns actually needed
The index's included columns must still genuinely match what's requested for this fix to work

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies SELECT * as the likely cause
Correctly explains why it defeats a covering index
Provides a correct fix naming specific columns

questions.title: A Count by Employee Shows the Same Number for Every Project
questions.prompt: In a Power BI model with CompanyProject, ProjectHours, and CompanyEmployee tables (ProjectHours in the middle, related to both), a visual counting distinct employees per project shows the identical number repeated for every project instead of varying counts. What's the likely cause, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: The likely cause is that the relationship between ProjectHours and CompanyEmployee is set to Single cross-filter direction, so filtering by CompanyProject reaches ProjectHours but doesn't continue through to CompanyEmployee — the employee count effectively ignores which project is selected and counts across the whole employee table every time, producing the same repeated number. The fix is to change that relationship's cross filter direction to Both, letting a filter from CompanyProject travel all the way through ProjectHours to CompanyEmployee. This works cleanly here because it's a simple star shape with ProjectHours in the center; if changing it to Both causes Power BI to reject the relationship or warn about ambiguity, that signals a loop elsewhere in the model (for instance, another path connecting CompanyProject and CompanyEmployee), which would need to be resolved separately, typically by marking one relationship inactive.
questions.professionalAnswer: The symptom — identical repeated numbers instead of varying ones — is the classic signature of a filter not actually reaching the table being counted, so that's where I'd look first, not at the DAX itself. I'd open Manage relationships and check the cross filter direction on the ProjectHours-to-CompanyEmployee relationship specifically, since that's the one standing between the project filter and the employee count. If it's set to Single, that's almost certainly it: a filter from CompanyProject reaches ProjectHours fine, but Single direction stops it from continuing on to CompanyEmployee, so the count of distinct employees just ignores the project filter entirely and returns the same whole-table number every time. Switching that relationship to Both should fix it immediately in a simple star-shaped model like this. If Power BI pushes back and won't let me set it to Both, or warns about ambiguous filtering, that tells me there's a second path connecting those two tables somewhere I haven't accounted for, and I'd need to find and break that loop before Both can safely apply.

Setting every relationship in the model to Both without checking for loops first, which can cause Power BI to reject the change
Not recognizing the 'identical repeated number' symptom as specifically a filter-not-reaching-the-table problem
Fixing this one relationship without checking whether other visuals in the report rely on the Single-direction behavior elsewhere
keyPoints: Single cross filter direction stops a filter from reaching past the immediate related table
The 'same number repeated everywhere' symptom indicates the filter isn't reaching the counted table at all
Both direction lets a filter in a simple star schema travel all the way through
A model with loops may reject Both and need an inactive relationship instead

Correctly explains why Single direction produces this exact symptom
Provides the correct fix (switch to Both)
Mentions the loop/ambiguity caveat

questions.title: A Scheduled Refresh Quietly Stopped Running
questions.prompt: A Power BI semantic model's scheduled refresh hasn't actually updated the data in over a week, but nobody got an obvious single alert about it being "turned off." What's the most likely explanation, and what are the two things you'd check first?
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely explanation is Power BI's four-failures rule: after four consecutive scheduled refresh failures, Power BI automatically disables the schedule, with no prominent standing banner beyond the failure emails that were sent at the time, which are easy to miss or filter out. The two things to check first are the gateway, since an outdated gateway version is behind a surprising number of otherwise-confusing refresh failures, and whether the report has a gateway selected at all, since the underlying data source may have changed or gone missing. After identifying and fixing the underlying cause — commonly expired credentials — re-enabling requires going back to Schedule refresh and manually flipping the toggle back on; simply fixing the root cause doesn't automatically turn a disabled schedule back on.
questions.professionalAnswer: The 'quietly stopped, no obvious single alert' detail is the real clue here, and it points straight at the four-failures rule: Power BI automatically disables a scheduled refresh after four consecutive failures, and the only trace of that is the failure emails that went out at the time, which are genuinely easy to miss, especially if the original owner isn't checking that inbox closely. Before I go hunting for anything exotic, the two things I'd check first are the basics the official troubleshooting guidance always starts with: is the gateway up to date, since an outdated gateway causes a surprising share of failures that look unrelated on the surface, and does this report even have a gateway selected right now, since a changed or removed data source would also silently break things. Once I find and fix whatever actually caused the failures — expired credentials being the most common culprit — I'd remember that fixing the cause alone doesn't turn the schedule back on; I have to go back into Schedule refresh and flip it on myself.
commonMistakes: Assuming a single obvious error or notification caused this, rather than the quiet four-failures auto-disable
Fixing the root cause (e.g. expired credentials) and assuming the schedule resumes automatically, without re-enabling it
Skipping the gateway-version check as 'too basic' before diagnosing something more complex
Not checking refresh history for the actual error message, which usually names the specific failure directly
keyPoints: Four consecutive failures auto-disable a scheduled refresh with no prominent standing alert
Check gateway version and whether a gateway is selected at all, before anything more exotic
Refresh history logs every attempt's status and error message
Fixing the cause doesn't re-enable the schedule -- that toggle must be flipped back on manually

Names the two basic checks (gateway version, gateway selected)
Notes refresh history as where to find the actual error
States that the schedule must be manually re-enabled after the fix

questions.title: The Pipeline Shows "Succeeded" Even Though a Copy Activity Failed
questions.prompt: An Azure Data Factory pipeline has a Copy activity whose Upon Failure path connects to a cleanup activity. Last night the Copy activity genuinely failed, the cleanup ran successfully, and the pipeline's overall run status still shows "Succeeded." Is this a bug? Explain what's actually happening and how you'd change the design if you want a failed Copy to make the whole pipeline show red.
questions.modelAnswer: This isn't a bug — it's the Try-Catch pattern behaving exactly as designed. Data Factory determines overall pipeline status only by looking at leaf activities, the ones with nothing connected downstream of them. Here, only Upon Failure is defined from the Copy activity, routing to the cleanup activity; there's no Upon Success or Upon Skip path defined from the Copy activity itself feeding into anything else, so the cleanup activity (which succeeded) is the only leaf activity Data Factory evaluates, and a successful leaf means the pipeline reports Succeeded — the Copy activity's own failure is absorbed rather than surfaced. To make a failed Copy actually show red at the pipeline level, switch to a Do-If-Else pattern: define both an Upon Failure path (to the cleanup/error handler) and an Upon Success path from the Copy activity, each leading to further downstream activities — with both paths now feeding leaf activities, a failure on the Copy activity side becomes a failure on a leaf activity, and the overall pipeline status reports Failure.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them it's genuinely not a bug, even though I understand why it looks like one at first glance — this is Try-Catch doing exactly what it's designed to do. The key detail is that Data Factory only looks at leaf activities — the ones with nothing after them — to decide whether the whole pipeline succeeded or failed. In this design, the only thing defined after the Copy activity is its Upon Failure path into the cleanup activity, so when the cleanup activity finishes successfully, that's the only leaf activity in the picture, and a successful leaf means a successful pipeline, full stop — the Copy activity's own failure never gets to 'vote' on the overall status because nothing is watching for it at the top level. If they want a failed Copy activity to actually make the pipeline go red — say, so a downstream alert fires — the fix is to switch to Do-If-Else: define both an Upon Failure and an Upon Success path out of the Copy activity, each leading somewhere, so now both outcomes are being tracked as leaf-level paths instead of only the failure path being absorbed by the handler.
commonMistakes: Assuming this is a bug in Data Factory rather than the designed behavior of leaf-activity status evaluation
Confusing the Try-Catch pattern (absorbs failure, reports success) with Do-If-Else (surfaces failure)
Not recognizing that only leaf activities (nothing downstream) determine overall pipeline status
Trying to fix this by adding more logging inside the cleanup activity instead of restructuring the activity paths
keyPoints: Pipeline status is determined only by leaf activities -- ones with nothing downstream
Try-Catch (only Upon Failure defined) absorbs the failure and reports overall success
Do-If-Else (both Upon Failure and Upon Success defined) surfaces the failure to the pipeline level
This is intended behavior, not a bug

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains this is intended Try-Catch behavior, not a bug
Correctly explains the leaf-activity status evaluation rule
Proposes the correct Do-If-Else fix
Explains why Do-If-Else changes the outcome

questions.title: A dbt Test Failure Just Blocked the Production Deploy
questions.prompt: A scheduled dbt job fails because a not_null test on customer_id in stg_orders returns 40 failing rows, and the production deploy is now blocked. Walk through how you'd diagnose whether this is a real data problem or a test that's too strict, and what you'd do before just disabling the test to unblock the deploy.
questions.modelAnswer: The first move is not disabling the test — that just hides the symptom somewhere harder to trace downstream. Instead, actually query the 40 failing rows directly (dbt can store failures in a dedicated table with --store-failures, or you can run the underlying test's compiled SQL manually) to see what's really in them: are these genuinely new orders missing a customer_id because of a real upstream source bug, or were they always expected to have no customer_id for a legitimate reason the test never accounted for, like guest checkout orders? If it's a genuine upstream data-quality problem, the fix belongs upstream, not in loosening the test. If the nulls are a legitimately expected case, the right fix is making the test reflect reality — for example, scoping it with a where clause that excludes guest orders — rather than removing not_null from the column entirely. Only once the cause is actually understood is adjusting or disabling the test an acceptable, deliberate decision, not a quick unblock.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't touch the test itself until I'd actually looked at what's failing. I'd pull the 40 rows — either by running the compiled test query directly or using --store-failures so they land in a queryable table — and look for a pattern: are these all from one source system, one time window, one order type? If they trace back to a genuine bug upstream, like a new order source that forgot to populate customer_id, that's the real fix, and the test did exactly its job by catching it before it shipped. If instead I find these 40 rows are all a known category — say, guest checkouts that have never had a customer_id by design — then the test itself was wrong to assume every order has one, and I'd fix the test, not weaken it blindly: add a where clause scoping not_null to orders where is_guest_checkout = false, rather than just deleting the test and losing coverage on the cases that genuinely matter. Either way, I'm documenting which one happened and why, so the next person who sees this test (or a similar failure) isn't starting from zero.
commonMistakes: Disabling or deleting the failing test immediately just to unblock the deploy, without understanding why it failed
Assuming the test itself is wrong before actually looking at the failing rows
Fixing the symptom by loosening the test instead of addressing a genuine upstream data problem
Adjusting or disabling a test without documenting why, leaving the next engineer confused about whether the exception is intentional
keyPoints: Investigate the actual failing rows before touching the test at all
Distinguish a genuine upstream data-quality problem from a test that misses a legitimate business scenario
Fix the root cause — upstream data or the test's own logic — rather than silencing the symptom
Any deliberate test adjustment should be documented, not a quiet unblock

Correctly distinguishes a real data problem from a too-strict test
Proposes fixing the actual root cause rather than the symptom
Mentions documenting any deliberate test change

questions.title: A Task Has Been Stuck in 'up_for_retry' for an Hour
questions.prompt: A task in a DAG you own has been sitting in up_for_retry state for over an hour, well past its retry_delay, and hasn't actually retried. The DAG run itself still shows as running. What would you check, in what order, to figure out why it isn't actually retrying?
questions.modelAnswer: First, check whether this is really a retry-timing issue or a scheduler problem — up_for_retry just means the task is waiting for the scheduler to re-queue it once retry_delay has passed, so the scheduler is the one actually responsible for acting on that; a stalled, crashed, or overloaded scheduler won't pick up any task waiting to retry, no matter how far past its delay it is. Second, check pool or worker-slot capacity — if the task's pool (or the executor's available worker slots) is fully occupied by other running tasks, a task that's eligible to retry still can't actually start until a slot frees up, which looks identical to 'stuck' but is really 'queued behind capacity.' Third, check DAG- and task-level concurrency settings like max_active_runs and task concurrency limits, since an overly restrictive limit can silently prevent an otherwise-ready task from starting even when the scheduler and workers are both healthy.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first instinct wouldn't be to look at the task's own retry settings — up_for_retry is a normal, boring state, and the question is really 'why hasn't the scheduler acted on it yet.' So first I'd check scheduler health itself: is it actually running, is it backed up, are other DAGs also showing delayed task pickup right now, which would point at a systemic scheduler problem rather than anything specific to this one task. Second, I'd check whether this task sits in a pool, and whether that pool (or the executor's worker slots generally) is fully saturated by other tasks — a task that's perfectly ready to retry still waits its turn if there's no slot open for it, and that's an extremely common cause that has nothing to do with the retry_delay setting at all. Third, I'd look at the DAG's own concurrency settings, because a restrictive max_active_runs or task-level concurrency limit can quietly block a task from starting even when everything upstream of it looks healthy. Only after ruling those three out would I start doubting the task's own retry configuration.
commonMistakes: Assuming the retry_delay setting itself is misconfigured before checking whether the scheduler or worker pool is actually healthy
Not checking pool/worker slot capacity, which can make a perfectly healthy task look permanently stuck
Restarting the whole DAG run instead of diagnosing the actual bottleneck first
Overlooking DAG-level concurrency settings (max_active_runs, task concurrency) that can silently block a ready task
keyPoints: up_for_retry means waiting for the scheduler to re-queue the task after retry_delay, not an error by itself
Check scheduler health first, since a stalled scheduler acts on no task at all
Check pool/worker slot capacity, which can block a ready task from actually starting
Check DAG/task-level concurrency settings that can silently prevent execution

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what up_for_retry actually means
Checks scheduler health as a first, logical step
Checks pool/worker capacity as a likely cause
Checks DAG/task concurrency settings

questions.title: Queries Got Slower and Credit Usage Barely Dropped After a Warehouse Resize
questions.prompt: A team resized its ETL virtual warehouse from Large down to Small to save credits, and now the nightly load takes three times as long while overall monthly credit consumption barely dropped. Explain what's likely happening and how you'd verify it.
questions.modelAnswer: Warehouse size determines available compute, roughly doubling with each size step up, so a Small warehouse genuinely has far less parallel processing power than a Large one — a workload that was comfortably parallelized across Large's resources will take meaningfully longer on Small, which is expected behavior, not a bug. The reason overall credits barely dropped despite that is that the lower per-second rate and the much longer runtime roughly cancel out: Snowflake bills per-second based on warehouse size, so halving the size while roughly tripling the runtime lands close to the same total credit cost for that job, especially once the minimum per-resume billing charge is factored in. To verify this, check QUERY_HISTORY (or the Snowsight warehouse activity view) for this specific nightly job before and after the resize, comparing both execution time and actual credits billed for those runs specifically — not just the end-of-month aggregate, which can be muddied by other warehouses' usage changing at the same time.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain this as the classic 'smaller isn't automatically cheaper' trap. Resizing down genuinely reduces available compute, and if this nightly load was actually benefiting from that extra parallelism on Large, running it on Small isn't just a little slower, it can be dramatically slower, especially for a job that was using many parallel threads over large data. The reason the bill didn't really improve is almost arithmetic: Snowflake bills per-second at a rate tied to warehouse size, so a job that now takes three times as long at roughly half the per-second rate nets out close to even, and the per-resume minimum billing only makes that worse if the job's actual working time barely changes while wall-clock time balloons. To actually verify this instead of guessing, I'd go straight to QUERY_HISTORY, filter to this specific job's query ID or tag both before and after the resize, and compare execution_time and credits_used_cloud_services/warehouse credits directly for those specific runs — the month-end total is too noisy to isolate one job's before-and-after picture.
commonMistakes: Assuming a smaller warehouse always saves money without checking whether the resulting longer runtime offsets the savings
Looking only at end-of-month aggregate credit totals instead of isolating this specific job's before/after usage
Not accounting for the per-resume minimum billing charge when a workload's run pattern changes
Resizing warehouses without first checking whether the actual workload (data volume, parallelism) justifies the change
keyPoints: Smaller warehouse size means meaningfully less available compute, directly increasing runtime for large or parallel workloads
Billing per-second at a lower rate over a longer runtime can roughly cancel out expected savings
Verify using QUERY_HISTORY for the specific job, not month-end aggregate totals
Right-sizing should match the actual workload's needs, not assume smaller is automatically cheaper

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why a smaller warehouse increases runtime
Correctly explains why total credits barely changed
Proposes a correct, specific way to verify using QUERY_HISTORY
Avoids blaming month-end aggregates alone

questions.title: Choosing a clustering key for a new fact-staging table
questions.prompt: You're designing a new staging table that will be loaded nightly and queried immediately afterward by ProductID ranges. A table can have only one clustered index. Explain the difference between a clustered and nonclustered index, and what makes a good choice of clustering key.
questions.modelAnswer: A clustered index determines the actual physical order rows are stored in on disk -- which is exactly why a table can have only one: data can only be physically sorted one way. A nonclustered index is a separate structure that holds a sorted copy of the indexed column(s) plus a pointer back to the actual row, and a table can have many of them. Looking up a row through the clustering key is fastest, since SQL Server navigates directly to the physical location; looking up through a nonclustered index takes one extra step -- find the index entry, then follow the pointer back to the row. A good clustering key is narrow (a small data type, since every nonclustered index secretly stores the clustering key as its row pointer), unique (no ambiguity about physical order), and ever-increasing (so new rows append at the end instead of forcing existing rows to physically shuffle). Given the staging table is loaded nightly and then range-queried by ProductID, an ever-increasing identity key for the clustered index, with a nonclustered index on ProductID to support the range queries, is the more defensible design than clustering directly on ProductID.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this as two separate decisions. First: what should the table's physical row order be -- that's the clustered index, and I only get one shot at it. Second: what other lookup patterns do I need to support cheaply -- that's where nonclustered indexes come in, and I can have several. For a staging table that's loaded nightly, I actually lean toward an ever-increasing identity column as the clustering key rather than ProductID directly, even though ProductID is the column people will query by. The reason is load performance: an ever-increasing key means new rows always append at the end of the physical order, so the nightly load doesn't cause page splits from inserting into the middle of existing data. Then I add a nonclustered index on ProductID to support the range queries -- yes, that costs one extra pointer-following step per lookup compared to clustering directly on ProductID, but it's a much smaller cost than the load-time page-splitting I'd get from clustering on a column that isn't naturally ordered or unique.
commonMistakes: Assuming more indexes are always better without considering the nightly load's insert cost
Choosing a wide, non-unique column as the clustering key, which bloats every nonclustered index that secretly carries it as a pointer
Forgetting a table can have only one clustered index, and trying to 'cluster' on two different columns
Not connecting the ever-increasing key recommendation to the specific nightly-load write pattern described in the scenario
keyPoints: Clustered index = physical row order, one per table
Nonclustered index = separate structure with a pointer back to the row, many allowed
Good clustering key: narrow, unique, ever-increasing
Design choice should weigh load (insert) pattern against query (read) pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the clustered vs. nonclustered distinction
Correctly lists the three traits of a good clustering key
Applies the tradeoff to the specific nightly-load scenario given
Recommends a nonclustered index to support the ProductID range queries

questions.title: Bridge table or a direct many-to-many relationship?
questions.prompt: Power BI allows a direct many-to-many relationship between two tables without building a bridge table yourself. Given that, explain when you'd still choose to build an explicit bridge table for a Sale-to-Salesperson relationship instead of just setting the relationship's cardinality to many-to-many directly.
questions.modelAnswer: Power BI's direct many-to-many relationship setting is convenient -- it lets two tables relate without an intermediate table, and Power BI handles the filtering internally. But it comes with real tradeoffs: it can be harder to reason about and debug when filter results look wrong, and it doesn't give you anywhere to attach additional information about the relationship itself -- a role, a credit percentage, a date the association started. An explicit bridge table is still the better choice whenever any of those matter: if a salesperson's credit on a sale isn't always equal (say, a 60/40 split between two reps), the bridge table is exactly where that percentage lives, as a real column -- a direct many-to-many relationship setting has no equivalent. A bridge table is also more transparent during debugging: you can literally query it and see the actual association rows, whereas a direct many-to-many relationship's behavior is more opaque. I'd default to a direct many-to-many relationship for a quick, simple case with no extra attributes needed, and build an explicit bridge table the moment the relationship itself needs to carry data or the model needs to be debuggable by someone besides me.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of the direct many-to-many setting as the quick path, and the bridge table as the path I take once the relationship itself needs to say more than just 'these two things are associated.' If all I need is 'this sale involved these salespeople,' with nothing else attached to that fact, the built-in many-to-many relationship setting is genuinely fine and saves me a table. But the moment the relationship needs its own data -- like a credit split percentage when a sale is shared 60/40 between two reps, or a 'role' on the sale like 'lead' vs. 'support' -- there's no column to put that on if I'm just flipping a cardinality setting; a bridge table, by contrast, is just a regular table, so I add CreditPercent or Role as columns on it without a second thought. I'd also reach for an explicit bridge table on anything a teammate besides me will need to maintain or debug, because 'query the bridge table and look at the rows' is a much easier thing to hand off than 'understand how Power BI's internal many-to-many filtering works.' So my actual rule is: default to the built-in setting for a quick, attribute-free case, and build the bridge table the moment the relationship needs to carry its own information or needs to be transparent to someone else on the team.
commonMistakes: Treating the built-in many-to-many setting and a bridge table as functionally identical in every case
Missing that a bridge table can hold its own attributes (credit percentage, role) while a direct relationship setting cannot
Defaulting to a bridge table every time without considering the simpler built-in setting is sufficient for a bare association
Not considering debuggability/maintainability by other teammates as a real factor in the decision
keyPoints: Power BI's direct many-to-many relationship setting handles a bare association without an extra table
A bridge table is still preferred when the relationship itself needs to carry attributes (credit %, role, date)
A bridge table is more transparent to query and debug than the internal behavior of a direct many-to-many relationship
The decision should be based on whether the relationship needs its own data, not just convenience

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what the built-in many-to-many relationship setting does
Correctly identifies that a bridge table can carry its own attributes and the direct setting can't
Correctly identifies debuggability/transparency as a reason to prefer a bridge table

questions.title: Views, or Raw Tables, as the Layer Power BI Connects To
questions.prompt: You're setting up a new Power BI semantic model that will query SQL Server directly. A teammate suggests pointing Power BI straight at the base tables. Would you recommend that, or a layer of views in between? Justify your answer.
questions.modelAnswer: A layer of views between the base tables and Power BI is generally the better design, for reasons that go beyond simple convenience. A view lets the BI layer depend on a stable, named contract — SELECT CustomerID, FirstName, LastName FROM dbo.vw_Customers — instead of depending directly on base table structure that database developers may need to change for unrelated reasons (renaming a column, splitting a table, adjusting a join elsewhere in the schema). As long as the view's output columns stay the same, the underlying tables can evolve without breaking the Power BI model at all. Views also let the database team pre-bake business logic once — a consistent definition of "active customer," a standard join eliminating duplicate rows — so every report built on top of vw_ActiveCustomers uses the identical, tested definition instead of each report author re-deriving (and potentially getting slightly wrong) the same logic independently. The tradeoff is an extra layer to maintain and document, and views add no meaningful performance cost since they're just saved SELECT statements executed live.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd recommend views, and the argument I'd actually make is about who owns the risk of changing the schema later. If Power BI points straight at base tables, any future change to those tables — even one that has nothing to do with reporting, like a database developer normalizing a column for an unrelated application feature — risks silently breaking the semantic model, because Power BI now depends on the table's exact current shape. A view sits in between as a stable contract: as long as vw_Customers keeps returning the same columns, the tables underneath it can be restructured freely without Power BI ever noticing. The second reason I'd give, maybe even more practical day to day, is that a view lets us define business logic once instead of every report builder re-deriving it slightly differently — one agreed, tested view of 'active customer' or 'current fiscal year sales,' instead of five dashboards each quietly defining it a little differently. The cost is one more layer to maintain, but for a model that's going to be queried repeatedly by BI tools, that cost is worth paying.
commonMistakes: Pointing Power BI directly at base tables, coupling the semantic model to unrelated schema changes
Not recognizing that a view is still a live query, not a copy, so it adds no real performance overhead
Letting each report author re-derive the same business logic slightly differently instead of standardizing it in a view
Treating the view layer as purely cosmetic rather than a genuine stability and consistency boundary
keyPoints: A view provides a stable contract, decoupling Power BI from base table schema changes
Business logic defined once in a view avoids multiple slightly-different report-level definitions
A view is a live query, not a data copy, so there's no meaningful performance tradeoff
The real cost is an added layer to maintain and document

Correctly explains the schema-decoupling benefit
Correctly explains the consistent-business-logic benefit

questions.title: Static Roles or Dynamic RLS for a Growing Sales Org
questions.prompt: A sales organization currently has 5 regions and wants row-level security so each regional manager only sees their own region's data. The VP mentions the company plans to expand to 40 territories within two years. Would you design static RLS roles or dynamic RLS, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: Dynamic RLS is the better design here, specifically because of the stated growth trajectory, even though static roles would technically work for 5 regions today. A static role defines one hardcoded filter per region (like [Region] = "West"), which means 5 regions require 5 separately created and separately maintained roles, each needing someone to manually assign the right people to it in the service. That approach doesn't scale cleanly to 40 territories — it means creating, testing, and maintaining 40 separate role definitions, and every org change (a new territory, a reassigned manager) becomes a manual update to a specific role rather than a data change. Dynamic RLS instead uses a single role whose filter expression, typically [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(), adapts automatically based on who's signed in, paired with a user-mapping table that pairs each person's email with their assigned territory. Scaling from 5 regions to 40 territories becomes a matter of adding rows to the mapping table, not creating new roles — which is exactly the maintenance burden the company's stated growth plan makes worth avoiding from the start.
questions.professionalAnswer: Given that the VP specifically mentioned 40 territories are coming within two years, I'd build dynamic RLS now rather than static roles, even though static would technically get the job done for just 5 regions today. The real argument is maintenance cost as this scales: a static role is one hardcoded filter per region, which means 5 regions is 5 separate roles I have to build, test, and separately assign people to in the service — and that same approach at 40 territories is 40 of everything, with every reorg or new hire meaning someone has to remember which specific role to update. Dynamic RLS sidesteps all of that: one role, with a filter like UserEmail = USERPRINCIPALNAME(), checked against a small mapping table that just pairs each person's email to their territory. Going from 5 regions to 40 territories under that design is literally just adding rows to a table, not building new roles — which is exactly the kind of growth the VP described, so I'd rather build the dynamic version now than redo this work in a year under time pressure.
commonMistakes: Choosing static roles because they're simpler for the current 5 regions, without weighing the stated growth plan
Forgetting that the user-mapping table's identity format must match what USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns in the service specifically
Assuming Test as role can fully validate how a specific other person will see the report (it only tests using your own identity)
Not considering the ongoing maintenance cost difference between 5 static roles and 40 static roles
keyPoints: Static roles require one separately maintained role per region/territory
Dynamic RLS uses one role whose filter adapts via a user-mapping table
Scaling dynamic RLS is a data change (add a row); scaling static RLS is a design change (add a role)
The stated growth plan is the deciding factor, not the current count alone

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recommends dynamic RLS with correct reasoning tied to the growth plan
Correctly explains the static-role scaling problem
Correctly describes the dynamic RLS mechanism (mapping table + USERPRINCIPALNAME)

questions.title: Import or DirectQuery for a New Finance Semantic Model
questions.prompt: Finance wants a new Power BI semantic model against a 15 GB SQL Server finance database, and insists the numbers must be "accurate to the second" because of same-day reconciliation. Would you choose Import or DirectQuery, and what would you tell them about the tradeoff?
questions.modelAnswer: This genuinely leans toward DirectQuery, because the stated requirement — accuracy to the second for same-day reconciliation — is precisely the scenario DirectQuery exists for: it queries the source live on every visual interaction, so there's no refresh lag at all, unlike Import, which is only ever as current as its last scheduled refresh. The real tradeoff to communicate honestly is that DirectQuery's visual speed depends entirely on the source database's own query performance, not on Power BI, so a 15 GB finance database with well-tuned indexes might feel fine, while an unoptimized one could make every click noticeably slower than Finance is used to. DirectQuery also restricts some DAX and modeling features compared to Import. A fair way to frame the decision for Finance: if genuinely real-time accuracy is non-negotiable, DirectQuery is correct and any slowness is a database performance problem to solve separately (indexing, query tuning) — but if "accurate to the second" really means "accurate as of this morning's refresh is fine, we just don't want stale numbers from last week," Import with a more frequent scheduled refresh solves the actual underlying need with none of DirectQuery's performance dependency.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd actually push back gently on the requirement first, because 'accurate to the second' and 'accurate as of today' get used interchangeably by stakeholders more often than people realize, and the right architecture is genuinely different depending on which one Finance actually means. If they truly need live, second-by-second accuracy — someone's actively reconciling intraday and a stale number would cause a real problem — that's DirectQuery, full stop, because Import can only ever be as fresh as its last refresh. But I'd be upfront about the real cost of that choice: DirectQuery's speed is entirely at the mercy of the source database's own performance, so if that finance database isn't well-indexed for the kinds of questions this report will ask, every click in the report inherits that slowness, and that's a database tuning problem, not something Power BI itself can fix. If it turns out 'accurate to the second' really just means 'not stale from last week,' I'd recommend Import with a tighter refresh schedule instead, since it gets them effectively the same practical outcome with far better report performance and full DAX feature support.
commonMistakes: Choosing Import by default without clarifying what 'accurate to the second' actually requires
Choosing DirectQuery without warning Finance that its speed depends entirely on the source database's own performance
Assuming DirectQuery always performs worse than Import, rather than it depending on the source's tuning
Not considering that converting DirectQuery to Import later is possible, but never the reverse
keyPoints: DirectQuery queries the source live; Import is only as current as its last refresh
DirectQuery's visual performance depends entirely on the source database's own speed
Clarifying what the stakeholder actually means by 'real-time' changes the correct architecture
Import generally offers fuller DAX/feature support than DirectQuery

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the Import vs. DirectQuery tradeoff
Makes a reasoned recommendation tied to the stated requirement
Flags the source-database-performance dependency honestly
Clarifies the ambiguity in 'accurate to the second' before committing

questions.title: Designing an Incremental Nightly Load for a Growing Table List
questions.prompt: A data team currently has five Azure Data Factory pipelines, one hardcoded per source table, copying each table nightly. The table list changes every few months as new sources are added. Propose a better pipeline design, and explain the tradeoff it introduces.
questions.modelAnswer: Five hardcoded, nearly-identical pipelines is a maintenance burden that grows every time a table is added or removed, since each change means building and testing a whole new pipeline rather than updating a configuration value. The better design is a single parameterized pipeline driven by a Lookup activity that reads the current table list from a configuration source — a control table, or a config file — with firstRowOnly set to false so it returns every row as an array, feeding a ForEach activity whose Items reference that array. Inside the ForEach, a single Copy activity, parameterized by @item() for the table name, handles the actual copy for whatever table that iteration is on. Adding or removing a source table becomes a one-row change to the configuration table, with zero changes to the pipeline itself. The tradeoff is that debugging becomes slightly less direct: a failure now surfaces inside a generic loop iteration rather than a pipeline with that table's name baked into it, and sequential-vs-parallel execution has to be decided carefully across all five-plus tables at once rather than independently per pipeline, since they now share one loop's settings.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd consolidate all five into one pipeline, driven by configuration rather than hardcoding each table into its own copy of nearly identical pipeline logic. The pattern is a Lookup activity at the start, reading the current table list from a small control table with firstRowOnly set to false so I get the whole list back as an array, feeding directly into a ForEach activity. Inside that ForEach, one Copy activity does the actual work, parameterized by @item() for whichever table that iteration is currently on. The real win is that adding the team's sixth or seventh source table six months from now becomes a single new row in a configuration table, with nobody touching the pipeline itself at all. I'd be upfront about the tradeoff, though: when something breaks at 2 AM, the error now says 'the ForEach iteration for table X failed' instead of 'the CustomerTable pipeline failed,' which is a half-step less direct to triage, and I'd also have to make one deliberate sequential-vs-parallel decision that now applies to every table in the list together, rather than being able to tune each pipeline's concurrency independently like before.
commonMistakes: Keeping five separate pipelines and just accepting the growing maintenance burden
Forgetting to set firstRowOnly to false on the Lookup, which would return only one row instead of the full table list
Not acknowledging the debugging tradeoff this consolidation introduces
Defaulting to parallel execution for all tables without checking whether any share a destination or resource
keyPoints: A Lookup activity with firstRowOnly: false feeds a ForEach the full table list
A single parameterized Copy activity inside the loop replaces five hardcoded pipelines
Adding a new source becomes a configuration change, not a pipeline change
The tradeoff is less direct debugging and a shared concurrency decision across all tables

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes the Lookup + ForEach + parameterized Copy pattern
Correctly explains how this reduces future maintenance
Honestly identifies a real tradeoff this design introduces
Mentions firstRowOnly: false as a necessary Lookup setting

questions.title: Choosing a Branching and Review Strategy for a Small BI Team
questions.prompt: A three-person BI team currently all commits directly to main, and a bad DAX change recently broke a shared report with no warning. Propose a branching and review strategy for this size of team, and explain why you wouldn't recommend something heavier.
questions.modelAnswer: For a three-person team, the right fix is a feature-branch-plus-pull-request workflow, not a heavier process built for a much larger org. Each change — a new report, a DAX fix, a model update — gets its own short-lived branch instead of a direct commit to main; when the work is ready, a pull request opens against main, giving the other two team members a place to actually review the change (ideally with at least one required approval before merge is allowed) and a checkpoint where any automated checks can run before the change reaches the shared report at all. This directly addresses the actual incident described: a bad DAX change landing straight on main with no review step is exactly what a required PR review would have caught before it ever reached production. The reason not to recommend something heavier — multiple long-lived environment branches, a formal change-advisory board, mandatory multi-approver sign-off — is that process overhead scales with team size and risk, and for three people on one shared codebase, a single main branch protected by required PR review already closes the actual gap without adding ceremony nobody has the staffing to sustain.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep this simple and proportional to the team's actual size, which is three people, not thirty. The fix for what just happened is a straightforward feature-branch-and-pull-request workflow: nobody commits straight to main anymore, every change gets its own branch, and a pull request is what actually merges it into main — with at least one of the other two team members required to approve before that merge button unlocks. That alone would have caught the exact incident they just had, because a second set of eyes on a DAX change before it reaches the shared report is specifically the gap that let a bad change through unreviewed. I'd deliberately stop there, though, and not reach for something heavier like multiple persistent environment branches or a formal review board, because that's process built for a much bigger org with a much bigger risk surface — for three people, a single protected main branch with required PR review closes the real gap without adding a weight of ceremony nobody on a three-person team has the bandwidth to actually sustain.
commonMistakes: Recommending a heavy multi-branch or formal-board process disproportionate to a three-person team
Proposing feature branches without also requiring at least one reviewer's approval before merge
Not tying the recommendation directly back to the specific incident (an unreviewed bad DAX change)
Assuming any branching strategy alone (without a required review gate) would have prevented the incident
keyPoints: Feature branches plus required pull-request review directly addresses unreviewed changes reaching main
A required approval gate is what actually catches a bad change before it ships
Process weight should scale with team size and actual risk, not be maximized by default
The recommendation should connect explicitly back to the real incident described

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes feature-branch + required PR review workflow
Explains how this specifically would have caught the described incident
Justifies not recommending a heavier process for this team size
Recommendation is concrete and actionable, not vague

questions.title: Enforcing the Layering Rules as a dbt Project Grows to 300 Models
questions.prompt: A dbt project has grown to roughly 300 models, and marts models have started referencing source() directly instead of going through staging, with business logic creeping into staging models too. Propose a concrete way to prevent this as the project keeps growing, beyond just asking people nicely in code review.
questions.modelAnswer: Code review catches some of this but doesn't scale reliably once a project has many contributors and hundreds of models — the fix has to be structural and automatable, not purely a matter of reviewer attentiveness. The concrete mechanism is a check run in CI against dbt's own project metadata: dbt's manifest (generated by dbt docs generate, or queried through a package like dbt_project_evaluator) can be used to assert rules like 'no model under models/marts/ directly calls source()' or 'every staging model has exactly one source() reference.' Running that check as a required CI step on every pull request turns the layering rule from something a reviewer has to remember into an automatic gate that blocks the PR if violated. Folder structure and naming conventions (stg_, int_, fct_/dim_) help contributors self-police, but the automated CI check is what actually enforces it reliably once no single reviewer can hold every rule for 300 models in their head.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd stop relying on reviewer memory the moment the project crossed roughly this size, because even a great reviewer misses things at 300 models across multiple contributors. The structural fix is to use dbt's own metadata against itself — the manifest (or a package like dbt_project_evaluator, which exists specifically for this) can answer questions like 'does any model under marts/ reference source() directly' or 'does any staging model reference another staging model instead of just its own source,' and I'd wire that check into CI as a required status check on every PR, not an optional lint someone can ignore. I'd pair that with the folder-and-naming convention, because that helps people do the right thing instinctively, but the convention alone is advisory — it's the automated, blocking CI check that actually guarantees the rule holds once the project is too big for any one person to review everything by eye.
commonMistakes: Relying solely on code review and documentation to enforce layering once the project is too large for any one reviewer to catch everything
Not using dbt's own project metadata (manifest / dbt_project_evaluator) to automate the check
Enforcing the rule only for new PRs going forward without addressing already-existing violations in the project
Treating folder naming conventions alone as sufficient enforcement, when they can be bypassed without an automated check
keyPoints: Manual code review doesn't scale reliably past a certain project size or contributor count
dbt's manifest/project metadata can be queried to enforce structural rules automatically
A required CI check turns a style guideline into an actual merge gate
Naming conventions help contributors self-police but are not a substitute for automated enforcement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes code review alone doesn't scale at this project size
Proposes using dbt's manifest/project metadata to automate the check
Proposes a required CI gate rather than an optional lint
Mentions naming conventions as a complement, not a substitute

questions.title: One Shared Warehouse, or Separate Warehouses per Workload?
questions.prompt: A company currently runs its nightly ELT loads and all its Power BI DirectQuery report traffic on the same single Snowflake virtual warehouse. Reports have started slowing down right when the nightly load runs. Propose a better warehouse architecture and explain the cost tradeoff it introduces.
questions.modelAnswer: The fix is workload isolation: give ELT and BI reporting their own separate virtual warehouses, even though both query the same underlying data. Because compute is fully decoupled from storage in Snowflake, two warehouses can run concurrently against identical tables without contending with each other at all — the nightly load running heavy on an ELT-dedicated warehouse no longer competes for the same compute that's trying to answer a report query at that same moment. Each warehouse can also be sized and auto-suspended independently for its own actual pattern: the ELT warehouse might reasonably run larger for a predictable overnight window then suspend, while the BI warehouse stays smaller but resumes instantly for unpredictable daytime report traffic. The tradeoff is that separating warehouses can modestly increase total credit usage, since each now has its own resume/suspend cycles and minimum billing increments instead of sharing one continuously-warm warehouse — but that's a predictable, budgetable cost increase in exchange for eliminating the unpredictable, user-facing report slowdowns the shared warehouse was causing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd separate these workloads onto their own warehouses, and I'd frame the decision around who's actually affected right now: report users are feeling the nightly load's resource contention every single night, and that's a real, recurring user experience problem, not just a theoretical inefficiency. Because Snowflake's compute is decoupled from storage, standing up a second warehouse costs nothing in terms of data duplication — both warehouses see the exact same tables — so this is purely a compute-isolation move. I'd size each warehouse for its own workload rather than both inheriting whatever the shared one used to be: the ELT warehouse can run larger and for a predictable window, then suspend; the BI warehouse can stay smaller since individual report queries don't need the same horsepower, but configured to resume instantly since report traffic is unpredictable through the day. The honest tradeoff to flag is that two separately-cycling warehouses will likely cost a bit more in aggregate credits than one continuously-shared warehouse would, mostly from independent resume/suspend overhead — but that's a known, budgetable cost against an unpredictable, user-facing problem that was actively frustrating people every night.
commonMistakes: Assuming more warehouses always costs proportionally more, without weighing resume-cycle overhead against the contention cost being eliminated
Sizing both new warehouses identically instead of matching each to its own workload's actual pattern
Not considering auto-suspend settings independently for each warehouse's own usage pattern
Treating this as purely a cost question without acknowledging the real user-facing performance problem being solved
keyPoints: Snowflake's compute/storage separation lets multiple warehouses query the same data without contending
Dedicated warehouses let ELT and BI workloads each be sized and suspended for their own pattern
Separating warehouses can modestly increase total credit cost from independent resume cycles
The tradeoff is predictable added cost versus eliminating unpredictable, user-facing contention

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes separate warehouses for ELT and BI workloads
Correctly explains why this eliminates the contention without duplicating data
Honestly identifies the real credit-cost tradeoff
Recommends sizing/suspend settings independently per workload
