questions.title: Triggering dbt From Airflow: a BashOperator, or the dbt Cloud API?
questions.prompt: You're designing a pipeline where Airflow orchestrates ingestion, then needs to trigger dbt transformations before a final export step. Would you run dbt directly inside Airflow (via a BashOperator or similar), or have Airflow trigger a dbt Cloud job through its API and poll for completion? Explain the tradeoff.
questions.modelAnswer: Both are legitimate, and the right choice depends on who owns dbt operationally and what visibility is actually needed where. Running dbt directly inside Airflow (via a BashOperator calling dbt run, or a dedicated operator) gives Airflow full, fine-grained control and visibility over every individual dbt model as its own step — per-model retries, per-model logs right inside the Airflow UI, one tool to check for the whole pipeline's status. The cost is that Airflow's own environment now needs the dbt project, its dependencies, and warehouse credentials available to it, and Airflow's workers end up doing dbt's compute-adjacent work directly. Triggering a dbt Cloud job via its API and polling for completion keeps the two tools cleanly separated — dbt Cloud owns its own execution environment, scheduling metadata, docs, and run history independently, and Airflow's job becomes a thin orchestration step: fire the job, poll until it finishes, proceed or fail based on the result. The tradeoff there is coarser visibility — Airflow only sees 'the dbt Cloud job succeeded or failed' as a single step, not each model's individual status, so debugging a specific model failure means leaving Airflow's UI for dbt Cloud's own run page.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask first who actually owns and debugs dbt day to day, because that drives the right answer more than any technical preference. If the data team lives in Airflow and wants per-model visibility and retry control right there in the same UI as everything else, running dbt directly — via a BashOperator or a purpose-built operator — gives them that, at the cost of Airflow's environment needing dbt's dependencies and warehouse credentials, and Airflow's own workers doing that compute-adjacent work. If dbt is run as its own well-governed service with its own scheduling, docs, and run history in dbt Cloud, I'd rather keep Airflow's job thin: call the API to kick off the job, poll for completion with a sane timeout, and treat the whole thing as one pass/fail step. The real cost of that second approach is that when something inside dbt fails, Airflow's UI just says 'the job failed' — it doesn't know or care which specific model broke — so whoever's on call needs to know to go look in dbt Cloud directly, which is a real debugging-workflow cost, not just a technical footnote.
commonMistakes: Assuming one approach is strictly better in all cases rather than weighing visibility against operational ownership
Running dbt directly inside Airflow without giving Airflow's environment the dbt project's dependencies and credentials it needs
Polling a dbt Cloud job without a sensible timeout, risking an Airflow task that waits indefinitely on a stuck job
Not considering who actually operates and debugs dbt day to day when choosing which tool should own the trigger
keyPoints: Running dbt inside Airflow gives per-model visibility and control but adds dbt dependencies/credentials to Airflow
Triggering dbt Cloud via API and polling keeps clean separation but gives only job-level, coarser visibility
The choice should reflect who operationally owns dbt and what debugging visibility is actually needed where
A polling-based trigger needs its own sensible timeout and retry handling

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the BashOperator/direct-run approach and its tradeoff
Correctly explains the dbt Cloud API/poll approach and its tradeoff
Ties the recommendation to operational ownership rather than a blanket preference
Mentions timeout/retry handling for the polling approach

questions.title: A stakeholder wants a new field added mid-sprint
questions.prompt: Your team is three days into a two-week sprint when a stakeholder asks you to add a new field to a report you're already building, saying it's 'quick, shouldn't change anything.' Walk me through how you'd actually handle this request.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't just say yes or no -- it describes a specific process for evaluating a mid-sprint request honestly before committing to it. First, actually assess the request rather than taking 'quick' at face value: does the new field require touching the dataset's underlying query, does it interact with existing filters or parameters, does it need its own testing? Second, be transparent with the stakeholder and the team about the real tradeoff: if it genuinely is small, say so and fold it in; if it's not, explain specifically why (not vaguely) and present the actual options -- add it now and risk the sprint's committed work, or add it to the next sprint, or (if it's urgent) swap it in for something already committed and explicitly deprioritized. The point to get across is that this isn't about being rigid or unhelpful -- it's about making the tradeoff visible instead of silently absorbing scope and then explaining later why other committed work slipped.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just say yes because it's described as quick, and I also wouldn't flatly refuse because 'that's not what we committed to' -- I'd actually go look at what the change requires first. If it really is a one-column addition to an existing dataset with no filter interactions, I'd just do it and move on, because treating every tiny request as a formal change-control event is its own kind of overhead. But if it touches the dataset's query, interacts with parameters already in play, or needs real testing, I'd say that specifically and honestly, rather than agreeing and then quietly having something else slip. I'd lay out the actual choice for the stakeholder and my Product Owner: we can add this now and something else committed to this sprint moves to next sprint, or this goes into the next sprint's backlog, or if it's genuinely urgent, I'll tell you specifically what I'd need to drop to make room for it. What I'm protecting isn't my own workload -- it's the team's ability to make an honest commitment and actually hit it, instead of everyone quietly absorbing 'just one more small thing' until the sprint's real scope bears no resemblance to what was planned.
commonMistakes: Automatically agreeing to the request without actually assessing its real scope first
Refusing rigidly without explaining the real tradeoff or offering alternatives
Silently absorbing the extra work and letting already-committed work slip without telling anyone why
Not involving the Product Owner or team in the actual tradeoff decision
keyPoints: Actually assesses the request's real scope instead of taking 'quick' at face value
Is transparent about the tradeoff rather than silently absorbing scope creep
Presents concrete options (do it now and drop something, defer it, or swap priorities)
Frames the goal as protecting the team's ability to make honest commitments, not personal workload

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes actually assessing the request's real scope rather than assuming
Shows transparent communication about the tradeoff involved
Presents concrete, realistic options rather than a flat yes/no
Frames this as protecting the team's commitments, not personal convenience

questions.title: Communicating a blocker in the daily standup
questions.prompt: You're stuck on a task -- a stored procedure change you need is waiting on another team's approval -- and it's been blocked for two days. How would you bring this up in the daily standup, and what would you do about it outside of standup?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats the Daily Scrum correctly -- as a short team sync, not a status report to a manager -- and keeps the standup update itself brief and specific: what's blocked, who or what it's waiting on, and how long it's been stuck, rather than a long explanation of the underlying technical problem. The real work happens outside standup: actually escalating the blocker rather than just mentioning it and waiting -- following up directly with whoever owns the approval, looping in the Scrum Master if the blocker is specifically the kind of cross-team obstacle they're meant to help clear, and being honest with the team about the sprint-goal impact if it stays stuck much longer, rather than quietly hoping it resolves itself. The key distinction a strong answer draws is between mentioning a blocker (passive) and actively working to clear it (what's actually expected).
questions.professionalAnswer: In standup itself, I'd keep it tight: 'I'm blocked on the stored procedure change -- it's been waiting on sign-off from the other team for two days now, and I don't have a resolution plan yet.' That's it -- standup isn't the place to walk through the technical details or vent about how annoying the wait is; it's a quick sync so the team knows where things stand. The actual work happens right after standup, not during it. I'd go directly to whoever on the other team owns that approval and ask specifically what's holding it up and when I can expect it, rather than just waiting passively for two more days. If that doesn't move things, I'd loop in my Scrum Master specifically, because clearing exactly this kind of cross-team blocker is their job, not something I should be expected to just push through alone. And if it looks like this is going to threaten the sprint goal, I'd say that out loud to the team well before the sprint review, not as a surprise at the end -- being blocked isn't a failure on my part, but sitting on it quietly without escalating would be.
commonMistakes: Treating the standup as the place to explain the full technical backstory instead of a brief status
Mentioning the blocker in standup but then passively waiting instead of actively escalating it afterward
Not involving the Scrum Master, whose job specifically includes clearing cross-team blockers
Waiting until the sprint review to surface that the blocker threatened the sprint goal
keyPoints: The Daily Scrum update should be brief and specific, not a technical deep dive
Mentioning a blocker in standup isn't the same as actively working to clear it
Escalating directly to the other team and/or the Scrum Master is the appropriate next step
Sprint-goal risk should be surfaced early, not held until the sprint review

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes an appropriately brief, specific standup update
Describes actively escalating the blocker outside of standup, not just waiting
Correctly involves the Scrum Master's actual role in clearing blockers
Shows early, honest communication about sprint-goal risk

questions.title: Two stakeholders both want their ticket done first
questions.prompt: You have two open tickets: a bug fix a sales manager is pushing for urgently, and a new report feature your own manager assigned last week with a deadline that's actually sooner. Both stakeholders think their request is the priority. How do you handle it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't unilaterally decide between two stakeholders' competing priorities on its own authority -- it recognizes that prioritization decisions belong with whoever actually owns the backlog's priority order (a Product Owner, in Scrum terms, or whoever plays that role on the team), and surfaces the conflict to them explicitly rather than quietly picking one and hoping the other doesn't notice. The practical first step is gathering the actual facts needed to make the decision -- how urgent is the bug really (is it actively breaking something for users right now, or just annoying), and what's the real deadline and consequence of missing it for the report feature -- rather than just taking either stakeholder's framing of urgency at face value. Then bring both pieces of information to whoever should decide, make the conflict and the tradeoff explicit, and get an actual decision rather than silently deprioritizing one person's request without them knowing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to quietly referee this myself between two people who each think their thing is most important -- that's not actually my call to make alone, and if I just pick one, I've effectively made a business priority decision without the authority or the full context to make it well. My first step is getting the real facts: is this bug actually breaking something in production right now, or is it an annoyance that feels urgent but isn't actually blocking anyone? What's the real, hard deadline on the report feature, and what actually happens if it slips a few days? Once I have real answers instead of just each stakeholder's own sense of urgency, I'd go to whoever actually owns prioritization for my work -- my manager, or a Product Owner if that's how the team is structured -- lay out both asks and their actual urgency side by side, and ask for an explicit call. I'd rather spend ten minutes getting a clear decision than spend a day guessing which stakeholder to disappoint and then having to explain that choice after the fact.
commonMistakes: Unilaterally deciding between two stakeholders' competing priorities without the authority or full context to do so
Taking either stakeholder's self-reported urgency at face value instead of verifying the actual impact and deadline
Quietly deprioritizing one request without telling that stakeholder, letting them find out later
Not escalating to whoever actually owns prioritization decisions for the team's work
keyPoints: Prioritization conflicts between stakeholders should be escalated, not unilaterally resolved
Gathers real facts about urgency and deadlines rather than accepting either framing at face value
Brings both pieces of information to whoever owns the priority decision for an explicit call
Avoids silently deprioritizing a stakeholder without their knowledge

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes this isn't a unilateral decision and escalates appropriately
Describes gathering real facts about urgency/impact before escalating
Describes a clear, explicit escalation with both pieces of information presented
Avoids silently disappointing either stakeholder without communication

questions.title: A ticket has no acceptance criteria
questions.prompt: You pick up a ticket from the sprint backlog that says 'Add a filter for region to the sales dashboard' with no further detail -- no acceptance criteria, no mention of default behavior or how it should interact with existing filters. What do you do before writing any code?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer resists the temptation to just start building based on a guess, because a story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done -- 'I think this is done' and a shared, checkable definition of done are different things, and building against the wrong assumption wastes real time for both the developer and whoever has to send it back. The right move is going back to whoever owns the ticket -- the Product Owner or the stakeholder who requested it -- and asking specific, concrete questions rather than one vague 'what do you mean': what should the filter's default value be, does it need to interact with (cascade from or into) any existing filters already on the dashboard, and is there a specific list of regions or should it reflect whatever's in the data. Writing those answers down as explicit acceptance criteria before starting, not after, turns a vague request into something both the developer and whoever reviews the finished work can actually check against.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start building off a guess, because 'add a filter for region' sounds simple but actually hides several real decisions -- what region data source is sensible as the dropdown's default, whether this filter needs to interact with any filter already on the dashboard, whether 'region' even means the same thing across every table the dashboard touches. Guessing wrong on any of those means I build something, it gets reviewed, and it comes back with changes -- which is slower overall than just asking upfront. So before writing anything, I'd go back to whoever owns the ticket with specific questions, not a vague 'can you clarify this' -- I'd ask directly: should this default to the viewer's own region if we track that, does selecting a region need to affect any other filter already on the page, and is there an existing region list I should match or is this open-ended. Once I have real answers, I'd write them down as the ticket's acceptance criteria myself if nobody else does, specifically so there's a shared, checkable definition everyone agrees to before I start -- that protects me too, since I now have something concrete to point back to if the request changes later.
commonMistakes: Starting to build based on a guess instead of clarifying ambiguous requirements first
Asking a vague 'can you clarify this ticket' instead of specific, concrete questions
Not writing down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting
Assuming the ticket's brevity means the request is actually simple, missing the real decisions hidden inside it
keyPoints: A story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done
Asks specific, concrete clarifying questions rather than a vague request for more detail
Writes down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting work
Clarifying upfront is faster overall than building on a guess and having it sent back

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes the ticket is too ambiguous to build from directly
Asks specific, concrete clarifying questions rather than a vague request
Describes writing down clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria
Explains why clarifying upfront saves time overall

questions.title: The Business Says the Dashboard You Built Isn't What They Asked For
questions.prompt: You finish a dashboard, it passes your own testing, and then the business stakeholder reviews it in UAT and says it doesn't actually answer what they needed. How do you respond, and how do you prevent the same gap next time?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats a UAT rejection as a normal, expected signal rather than a personal failure or a sign the stakeholder is being difficult — UAT exists specifically to catch the case where code is technically correct but isn't actually what the business needed, which is a different question than QA's "does it work correctly" entirely. The right immediate response is to ask specific, concrete questions rather than getting defensive: what exactly does the current version show, what were they expecting instead, and can they point to a specific number or view that's wrong relative to their mental model. Often the real gap traces back to acceptance criteria that were vague or incomplete at the start, not a build mistake — which is the actual thing to fix going forward: writing more specific, checkable acceptance criteria during intake (edge cases included, like what a zero-sales region should display) so UAT becomes a confirmation step rather than where requirements gaps first surface.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd do is not get defensive about it, because UAT rejecting something isn't the same as me having done something wrong — it's literally what that stage is for, catching the gap between 'this is technically correct' and 'this is actually what we needed,' which are genuinely different questions. I'd ask specific questions rather than just apologizing and reworking blindly: what exactly were you expecting to see here, can you show me a specific number that looks wrong to you versus what you expected. Usually when I dig into it, the real root cause isn't that I built the wrong thing technically — it's that the original request or acceptance criteria were vague enough that I made a reasonable assumption that just wasn't the assumption they were making. Going forward, the actual fix isn't 'be more careful next time,' it's writing tighter, more specific acceptance criteria up front — including the edge cases, like what happens when a region has zero sales for the month — so that gap gets caught during planning instead of surfacing for the first time in UAT.
commonMistakes: Treating a UAT rejection as a personal failure or getting defensive instead of investigating specifically
Reworking the dashboard based on a vague complaint without asking specific clarifying questions first
Not tracing the root cause back to incomplete acceptance criteria, repeating the same gap on the next project
Assuming the stakeholder is simply wrong instead of taking their feedback as a genuine signal about the request
keyPoints: UAT exists specifically to catch 'technically correct but not what was needed,' a different question than QA
The right response is specific clarifying questions, not defensiveness or blind rework
The root cause is often vague acceptance criteria at intake, not a build mistake
The real fix is tighter acceptance criteria going forward, including edge cases

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Responds professionally and non-defensively to the rejection
Describes asking specific clarifying questions
Correctly identifies the likely root cause (acceptance criteria gap)
Proposes a concrete prevention for next time

questions.title: Giving Feedback on a Teammate's Dashboard Before It Ships
questions.prompt: A teammate asks you to review their new dashboard before it goes to the business for UAT. You notice a DAX measure that will give misleading results for one specific filter combination, plus a few minor formatting inconsistencies. How do you give this feedback?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer distinguishes between the two issues by severity and handles each appropriately, rather than treating all feedback the same way. The DAX measure that produces misleading results under a specific filter combination is a genuine correctness issue that should block shipping until it's fixed — this gets flagged clearly and specifically, with the exact filter combination that triggers it and why, so the teammate can reproduce and verify the fix themselves rather than just taking it on faith. The formatting inconsistencies are real but minor, worth mentioning so the final product looks polished, but not something to present with the same urgency as a correctness bug, since conflating a blocking issue with cosmetic nitpicks can bury the important feedback or make the whole review feel more negative than it needs to be. Throughout, the feedback should be specific and actionable (showing the exact scenario, ideally suggesting a fix) rather than vague criticism, and framed around the shared goal of the dashboard being correct and ready, not as a personal judgment of the teammate's work.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd separate these two issues immediately in how I present them, because they're not the same kind of problem. The DAX measure is the one that actually matters before this goes anywhere near UAT — I'd show them the exact filter combination that breaks it, walk through why it produces a misleading number in that specific case, and treat that as something we fix before this ships, not an optional suggestion. I'd try to make that concrete enough that they can reproduce it themselves in two minutes rather than just trusting me that something's wrong. The formatting stuff I'd mention too, because it's worth cleaning up before the business sees it, but I'd deliberately keep it in a separate, lower-key category — a quick 'oh, and a few small formatting things, nothing urgent' rather than bundling it in with the real bug, because if I present both with equal weight, the actual correctness issue risks getting lost in a list that reads as nitpicking. I'd also frame the whole thing as 'let's get this right before UAT' rather than anything that reads as me judging their work.
commonMistakes: Treating a correctness bug and minor formatting notes with the same urgency, burying the important issue
Giving vague feedback ('something seems off with that measure') instead of a specific, reproducible scenario
Framing feedback as a personal criticism rather than a shared goal of shipping something correct
Not actually verifying the DAX issue is real before raising it, or not suggesting a direction for the fix
keyPoints: Correctness issues and minor polish issues should be flagged with different urgency
Feedback on a bug should be specific and reproducible, not vague
The framing should center on the shared goal (a correct, ready dashboard), not personal judgment
A genuine correctness issue should block shipping until resolved

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Distinguishes the correctness bug from the minor formatting issues appropriately
Describes giving specific, reproducible feedback on the DAX issue
Frames the feedback constructively around a shared goal
Correctly treats the correctness issue as blocking

questions.title: Receiving Pointed Feedback on Your Own SQL in a Pull Request
questions.prompt: You open a pull request with a new T-SQL view, confident it's correct. A senior teammate leaves a pointed comment: "This JOIN will double-count revenue whenever an order has more than one line item — did you test this against real data?" How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats this as useful, correct technical feedback to actually verify, not as a tone problem to get defensive about, even though the comment reads a little sharp. The right first move is to actually check the claim against real data rather than arguing or immediately agreeing out of deference — running the query against a test order known to have multiple line items and confirming whether revenue is in fact double-counted. If the reviewer is right, which a join producing row-level duplication against a different grain often is, the response is a straightforward acknowledgment and a fix, not an excuse, and ideally a brief note on what testing step would have caught this before opening the PR (so the lesson generalizes beyond this one query). If, after checking, the claim turns out to be wrong, the response is still calm and specific: showing the actual test data and result that demonstrates the join is correct, rather than taking either the criticism or one's own original confidence at face value.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first reaction wouldn't be to get defensive about the tone — it would be to actually go test what they're describing, because it's a specific, checkable technical claim, and the only thing that actually matters here is whether it's true. I'd grab (or construct) an order with two or three line items and run the query against it specifically, checking whether the revenue total for that order comes out right or genuinely doubled. If they're right, which is honestly pretty likely given how common this exact mistake is when joining a header table to a detail table without aggregating first, I'd just say so directly — 'you're right, confirmed it with a multi-line-item order, fixing it now' — and actually fix it, rather than getting into any back-and-forth about whether the comment was blunt. If I test it and it turns out the join is actually fine for some reason they didn't account for, I'd show them the specific test case and result that proves it, calmly, rather than either caving to seniority or digging in defensively without evidence either way.
commonMistakes: Getting defensive about the comment's tone instead of verifying the actual technical claim
Agreeing immediately out of deference to seniority without actually testing the claim
Dismissing the feedback without testing it, assuming the original code must be correct
Fixing the issue without understanding why it happened, risking the same mistake on a future query
keyPoints: The right first step is verifying the specific technical claim against real data
A correct criticism should be acknowledged directly and fixed, not argued with
If the claim turns out wrong, the response should be a calm, evidence-based explanation
The goal is determining what's true, not managing how the feedback felt

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Responds by verifying the claim rather than reacting to tone
Describes a concrete way to test the claim
Shows how to respond if the criticism is correct
Shows how to respond if the criticism turns out incorrect

questions.title: A Dashboard Goes Live, and Immediately Something's Wrong
questions.prompt: Two days after a new regional revenue dashboard launches, a regional manager reports it's showing zero sales for their region, which is obviously wrong. Walk through how you'd investigate this and what you'd communicate to the regional manager while you're still figuring it out.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates the investigation from the communication, and gets both moving in parallel rather than going silent until the fix is found. On investigation, the logical order is checking the environments closest to the symptom first: is this specific region's data actually present in the underlying source as of the relevant date, did the scheduled refresh for this model actually complete successfully (checking refresh history for errors), and does any report-level filter (RLS, a regional filter default) unintentionally exclude this region's rows. On communication, the mistake to avoid is going quiet until the root cause is fully found — the right move is an immediate, honest acknowledgment that specifically names what's being checked ("I've confirmed the issue and I'm checking whether it's a refresh failure or a filter problem, I'll update you within the hour") rather than either a vague "looking into it" or disappearing until there's a complete answer, since a specific update lets the regional manager decide what to do in the meantime (for example, whether to trust other numbers from the same report).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd do two things essentially at the same time: start investigating, and send the regional manager something specific right away rather than going quiet until I have a full answer. On the investigation side, I'd work from the symptom outward — first checking refresh history to see whether last night's scheduled refresh for this model actually succeeded, since a failed or partial refresh is a really common cause of 'this one region looks wrong.' If the refresh is fine, I'd check whether the region's data is actually present in the source table for the relevant date, and then check whether any filter — RLS, a default slicer, anything report-level — is quietly excluding that region specifically. On the communication side, I'd send something concrete almost immediately, like 'I've confirmed something's wrong with the regional number, I'm checking whether it's a refresh issue or a filter issue right now, I'll have an update for you within the hour' — specific enough that they know I've actually looked at it and know roughly when to expect more, rather than a vague 'we're on it' that tells them nothing.
commonMistakes: Going silent until the root cause is fully found instead of sending a specific interim update
Guessing at the cause instead of checking refresh history and filters methodically
Sending a vague 'we're looking into it' instead of naming what's specifically being checked
Fixing the symptom without identifying why it happened, risking a repeat next refresh cycle
keyPoints: Investigation and communication should happen in parallel, not sequentially
A methodical check order: refresh history, source data presence, then report-level filters
A specific interim update is far more useful than a vague one or silence
The regional manager should know roughly when to expect a further update

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a methodical, logically ordered investigation
Describes a specific, honest interim communication, not silence or vagueness
Recognizes investigation and communication should happen together
Mentions follow-up to prevent recurrence

questions.title: Explaining Why the Dashboard Can't Be Real-Time
questions.prompt: A non-technical executive asks why the sales dashboard doesn't update "the second a sale happens," and wants it changed to be fully real-time. How do you explain the actual tradeoff involved, without just saying no?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer avoids both extremes — flatly refusing, or agreeing to something without explaining the real cost — and instead translates the technical tradeoff into terms the executive actually cares about. The honest explanation is that the current dashboard uses Import mode, refreshing on a schedule, which is fast and fully featured but only as current as its last refresh; a genuinely real-time version would mean DirectQuery, querying the live source database on every single click, which can work but makes the dashboard's speed entirely dependent on the source database's own performance under that load, and may restrict some existing features. The better response is to find out what the executive actually needs underneath the stated request — is a slight delay (refreshing every 15-30 minutes instead of nightly) actually sufficient for the real business decision they're making, since that's a far smaller, lower-risk change than true real-time, which should be reserved for cases where it's genuinely necessary and worth its tradeoffs.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just say no, and I also wouldn't pretend there's no real tradeoff here, because there genuinely is one. I'd explain it in terms that matter to them rather than jargon: right now the dashboard is fast and has every feature we've built because it works off a saved snapshot that updates on a schedule, and making it truly real-time means it would instead ask the live database a question every single time someone clicks anything, which can work, but it means the dashboard's speed from then on depends entirely on how fast that production database can answer, and a database built for running the business, not for being hammered with report queries all day, might start to feel the strain. The question I'd actually ask back is what's really driving this — is it that last night's data feels stale for a decision they're making right now? Because if so, refreshing every 15 or 30 minutes instead of overnight might solve the actual problem with almost none of the real cost or risk that full real-time would introduce, and I'd rather find that out than build the expensive version for a need that a cheaper fix would also solve.
commonMistakes: Simply refusing the request without explaining the real tradeoff in terms the executive understands
Agreeing to build it without explaining the performance and feature risks involved
Using technical jargon (DirectQuery, storage mode) without translating it to business impact
Not asking what the executive actually needs underneath the stated 'real-time' request
keyPoints: The tradeoff should be explained in terms of business impact, not technical jargon alone
True real-time (DirectQuery) ties dashboard speed to the source database's live performance
The underlying need is often solvable with a more frequent refresh, not full real-time
Asking what's actually driving the request avoids over-building for a need a smaller fix would solve

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the real tradeoff clearly in non-technical terms
Avoids flatly refusing or agreeing without explanation
Investigates the underlying need behind the stated request
Proposes a reasonable alternative (more frequent refresh) where appropriate

questions.title: Explaining to a Stakeholder Why Their Dashboard Data Is a Day Late Because of a Failed dbt Test
questions.prompt: A dbt test failure blocked this morning's scheduled deploy, which means a stakeholder's dashboard is showing yesterday's numbers instead of refreshed ones, and they're asking why. Walk through how you'd explain this, and what you'd do about the underlying test failure in parallel.
questions.modelAnswer: The explanation to the stakeholder should be honest and specific, framing the blocked deploy as the system working correctly rather than something broken: a data-quality check caught a problem in this morning's data before it could reach their dashboard, so the deploy was intentionally held rather than publishing numbers that might be wrong — stale-but-trustworthy beats fresh-but-possibly-wrong. The update should name specifically what's being checked and roughly when to expect resolution, rather than a vague 'there's an issue.' In parallel, actually investigate the failing test the way any test failure deserves — determining whether it's a genuine upstream data problem or a test that doesn't match a legitimate new scenario — and only unblock the deploy once that's understood, not simply to shorten the stakeholder's wait. This is also a natural moment to set expectations going forward: that this is exactly what the testing exists to do, and an occasional held deploy is the acceptable tradeoff for never shipping numbers that haven't been verified.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them directly and specifically what happened: 'This morning's data didn't pass one of our automated quality checks, so we held the refresh rather than publish numbers that might be wrong — yesterday's data is accurate, just not current, and I'm actively looking into today's issue right now.' I wouldn't apologize as if the system failing safe was itself the failure — that framing matters, because it's the opposite of what actually happened. In parallel with that message, I'd go investigate the test the same way I would any other failure, figuring out whether it's a genuine upstream data problem or a test that doesn't account for something legitimate, and I'd resolve that properly rather than rushing to unblock the deploy just because someone's waiting. I'd also use the moment, once things are calm again, to set the expectation that this will happen occasionally, and that it's the system protecting them from something worse — a dashboard quietly showing wrong numbers with no warning at all.
commonMistakes: Apologizing as if the blocked deploy itself was a failure, instead of explaining it as the quality check working as designed
Giving a vague, non-specific explanation that leaves the stakeholder unsure when to expect fresh data
Rushing to unblock the deploy to satisfy the stakeholder before actually understanding the test failure
Not using the moment to set expectations about the stale-but-trustworthy tradeoff going forward
keyPoints: A blocked deploy from a failing test is the system working as intended, not a malfunction
The stakeholder explanation should be specific and honest, not vague or defensive
Investigate and resolve the actual test failure in parallel, not just to shorten the stakeholder's wait
Use the moment to set expectations about the stale-but-trustworthy tradeoff

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Frames the blocked deploy accurately as the system working correctly
Gives a specific, honest interim communication rather than a vague one
Describes investigating the actual test failure properly, not rushing to unblock
Sets reasonable expectations going forward

questions.title: A Stakeholder Wants You to Just Run Some Quick SQL Instead of Going Through dbt
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks you to just write a quick ad-hoc SQL query against the raw source tables to get them a number by end of day, bypassing the dbt models and tests your team maintains. How do you handle this, balancing their urgency against the governance your team has built?
questions.modelAnswer: The right response is neither a flat refusal nor quietly going around the governed models — it's understanding what's actually needed and finding the smallest safe path there. First, ask what the number is actually for and how precise or durable it needs to be: if it's a rough, one-time gut check for an internal conversation, a clearly-labeled ad-hoc query might genuinely be fine, as long as it's communicated upfront that it skips the tested, documented models and could disagree with the 'official' number later for reasons that haven't been checked, like duplicate rows or a status filter the models apply that this query doesn't. If the number is going to be repeated, shared further, or treated as authoritative, push back specifically on hitting raw tables and instead either query through existing tested marts if they already cover the need, or treat the request as a sign that a small, properly tested model is actually what's needed rather than a one-off query that quietly becomes a permanent habit nobody remembers is ungoverned.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't say an automatic yes or an automatic no — I'd ask what this number is actually for first, because that changes everything about how I'd respond. If it's genuinely a one-time number for an internal gut-check conversation that won't be repeated or shared further, I'd write the quick query, but I'd say out loud that it bypasses our tested models, so it might not perfectly match the 'official' number later, and that's an acceptable tradeoff for a one-off. If it sounds like this is going to become a recurring ask, or get shared outside the room, I'd push back specifically on using raw tables for it — either there's already a mart that answers this and I should just query that, or this is actually a sign we need a small, properly tested model rather than a habit of quietly running ungoverned SQL every time someone's in a hurry. What I'm trying to avoid is becoming the person who ships unverified numbers whenever someone asks nicely, while still being genuinely helpful under real time pressure rather than hiding behind process.
commonMistakes: Flatly refusing without understanding what the number is actually needed for
Silently running the ad-hoc query against raw tables without flagging that it bypasses tested models
Letting a 'quick one-time' ad-hoc query quietly become a recurring, ungoverned habit
Not offering an alternative — an existing mart, or a small tested model — when one would actually fit
keyPoints: Understand the actual urgency and intended use before deciding how to respond
Be transparent when a number bypasses tested, governed models, rather than quietly complying
Prefer existing tested marts over raw tables whenever they already answer the need
Watch for a 'one-time' ad-hoc request quietly becoming a recurring ungoverned pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Investigates the actual need and urgency rather than reacting automatically
Is transparent about the governance tradeoff rather than silently complying
Proposes a concrete alternative when one fits (existing mart or small tested model)
Balances helpfulness with protecting data governance, not just enforcing rules

questions.title: A Teammate Wants to Put Business Logic in a Staging Model 'Just This Once'
questions.prompt: A teammate's pull request adds a business-logic CASE statement (classifying order status into broader categories) directly inside a staging model, arguing it's simpler than adding an intermediate model for 'just one column.' You disagree with where it belongs. How do you raise this in code review?
questions.modelAnswer: The feedback should point to the actual downstream consequence rather than just citing a convention: once business logic lives in a staging model, every other mart that also needs that classification either duplicates the same CASE statement or reaches back into staging in an inconsistent way, and if the business definition changes later, someone has to remember it lives in a staging model instead of where they'd naturally look for it — an intermediate or marts model. The response should also acknowledge the real tradeoff being raised — yes, one more model file is more ceremony for a single column — while explaining that the convention exists specifically so nobody has to remember which staging models secretly contain hidden business logic and which don't; consistency has more value at project scale than saving one file for one column. The comment should suggest a concrete alternative, like a small intermediate model, rather than just disagreeing in the abstract, so the review feedback is actionable.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the comment around the consequence, not the rule: 'If this classification logic lives here, the next mart that also needs it either copies this exact CASE statement or has to reach back into a staging model to get business logic, which is exactly what staging models aren't supposed to carry. If the category definitions change later, someone has to remember they live here instead of in an intermediate or marts model, which is where anyone would naturally look first.' I'd also say I get the instinct — one more file does feel like overhead for a single column — but the whole point of the convention is that nobody should have to remember which staging models secretly got an exception; consistency pays off more as the project grows than the one file we'd save here. Then I'd suggest the actual fix rather than just leaving the objection hanging: pull this CASE statement into a small int_orders_classified model (or push it one layer out into an existing intermediate model if one already touches this), so staging stays what everyone expects it to be.
commonMistakes: Citing the layering convention without explaining the actual downstream consequence of violating it
Dismissing the teammate's 'it's just one column' point instead of acknowledging the real tradeoff they're raising
Blocking the PR without suggesting a concrete, actionable alternative implementation
Letting the exception through 'just this once' with no comment, inviting the same shortcut to spread
keyPoints: Explain the concrete downstream consequence (duplicated or inconsistent logic) rather than just citing the rule
Acknowledge the real tradeoff the teammate is raising instead of dismissing it outright
Offer a specific, actionable alternative (an intermediate model) rather than only disagreeing
Consistency at project scale outweighs the convenience of a one-off exception

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the concrete downstream consequence of the violation
Acknowledges the teammate's tradeoff rather than dismissing it
Offers a specific, actionable alternative implementation
Keeps the feedback constructive and professional
